strengths: The paper presents a clear and meaningful alternative to timestamp-token generation: ordered event/transition tokens are grounded to frames through a contrastive objective, while query-focused captioning injects event-specific semantics.

The empirical scope is strong, covering grounding, summarization, action localization, dense captioning, moment retrieval, highlight detection, and grounded reasoning across E.T.Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights.
Controlled comparisons are a major strength: competing architectures are retrained on the same E.T.Instruct data, and replacing their boundary-centric mechanisms with MeCo yields broad improvements.

The ablations support both principal components. Transition tokens substantially improve holistic segmentation, and informative query-focused captions outperform query copying; the captioning benefit is also shown to depend on the localization mechanism.

Results are competitive and often substantially better despite parameter-efficient one-epoch tuning and a relatively small 3.8B backbone. The especially large QVHighlights multi-segment retrieval gains are compelling.
The method, objectives, inference procedure, prompts, architecture adaptations, and core hyperparameters are described reasonably well, and no significant ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The description of MeCo as “timestamp-free” or eliminating boundary information is overstated. Training explicitly uses ground-truth start/end timestamps to construct segments, supervise every frame-token association, and extract clips for caption generation. The contribution eliminates boundary generation at inference, not boundary supervision.

The evaluation lacks comparisons against strong task-specific temporal grounding, highlight-detection, and dense-captioning models. Comparisons are concentrated on video LLMs, so the broader significance of MeCo as a temporal-localization approach remains unclear.

Important inference and evaluation choices are under-specified, including how thresholds are selected for multi-segment retrieval and CLIP baselines, the numerical threshold values, handling of overlapping or adjacent annotations, malformed structural-token sequences, and fragmented frame assignments. These choices can materially affect localization scores.

Query-focused caption supervision is produced from ground-truth-trimmed clips using MiniCPM-V-2.6 and GPT-4o-mini, but caption quality, hallucination rates, sensitivity to the captioning teacher, and additional generation cost are not evaluated. This weakens attribution of gains specifically to the proposed semantic mechanism.

The main ablations report averages over heterogeneous tasks, which can conceal regressions and metric-scale differences. Per-task component ablations, variance across training seeds, and statistical uncertainty are absent.

Some central claims are broader than the evidence: MeCo is not best on every reported metric, and scaling from 3.8B to 7B produces regressions on measures such as temporal event matching. Robustness to longer videos, sampling rates other than 1 fps, boundary precision, and out-of-domain data is also not studied.

Reproducibility is incomplete because preprocessing details for pseudo-caption generation, threshold calibration, caption prompts/settings, and failure-handling rules are insufficiently specified, despite otherwise useful hyperparameter and prompt documentation.

strengths: The structural-token formulation is a clear and potentially useful alternative to directly generating numerical timestamps. Modeling event and transition regions jointly is intuitive, and the grounding objective is technically plausible.
The empirical scope is relatively broad: the paper evaluates grounding, dense captioning, highlight detection, and grounded reasoning across E.T.Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights.

Several results are substantial, especially on E.T.Bench and QVHighlights. Controlled comparisons using E.T.Instruct and adaptations of existing architectures provide better evidence than comparisons only against published checkpoints.

The ablations examine transition tokens, query-focused captioning, query copying, and compatibility with multiple localization mechanisms. These generally support the importance of the proposed components.
The paper is organized clearly, provides inference pseudocode and training hyperparameters, and communicates the main intuition effectively.
weaknesses: The comparison is not fully controlled because MeCo receives additional pseudo-supervision generated from ground-truth event clips using MiniCPM-V and GPT-4o-mini, whereas the principal baselines receive only E.T.Instruct. This added supervision and external-model computation could explain part of the gains. Applying QFC to architectures for which it is poorly suited does not replace a data-equivalent control, such as adding comparably rich synthetic supervision to each baseline.

Important inference and evaluation details are missing. The threshold used for multi-segment retrieval is unspecified, as are its selection protocol, segment scoring and ranking for mAP, post-processing, and handling of duplicate or disconnected regions. QVHighlights performance can be highly sensitive to these choices, so the strongest reported improvement is difficult to reproduce or audit.

The method assumes that queried events and transitions form an ordered, non-overlapping partition of the entire video. The paper does not explain how it constructs targets when events overlap, coincide, touch video boundaries, or have ambiguous ordering—common cases in action-localization and dense-captioning datasets. It also does not analyze structural-token count errors.

The experimental positioning is incomplete. Comparisons focus almost entirely on video-LLM timestamp methods and omit strong specialist temporal-grounding, action-localization, and highlight-detection models on the standard benchmarks. Consequently, the broader claims about temporal localization effectiveness are not established.

The claim of consistent superiority is overstated: MeCo is below or tied with prior methods on some metrics, including Charades-STA R@1 at IoU 0.7 for the 3.8B model. Results are reported from single runs without uncertainty, significance testing, or sensitivity analysis for thresholds and frame sampling.

Query-focused captioning autoregressively generates substantial text before each event token, but the paper reports no latency, memory, token-count, or training-cost comparison. This omission is important because the method may trade timestamp-generation difficulty for much greater inference cost.

The phrase “timestamp-free” is potentially misleading. Ground-truth timestamps are still required to create training segments, and inference ultimately converts frame-level assignments back into temporal intervals; the contribution avoids timestamp token generation rather than timestamp supervision or boundary estimation.

Reproducibility is limited by the absent code URL, dependence on proprietary GPT-generated annotations, and lack of a stated release for the generated captions. There is also little discussion of caption-model errors, hallucinated pseudo-labels, dataset bias, or limitations. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but these evaluation and reproducibility gaps keep the evidence slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and meaningful alternative to boundary-token generation: contextual event and transition tokens are grounded to frames, while query-focused captions inject event-specific semantics. This is well motivated and technically coherent.

The empirical improvements are substantial and broad. Under matched E.T.Instruct training, MeCo improves over multiple temporal-localization video LLMs across grounding, dense captioning, and complex reasoning, with especially strong gains on TVG and multi-segment QVHighlights retrieval.

Controlled experiments strengthen the central claim: replacing the localization mechanisms of TimeChat and E.T.Chat with MeCo improves all reported aggregate metrics, while ablations separately demonstrate the importance of transition tokens and query-focused captioning.

Evaluation covers diverse tasks and datasets, includes two model scales, and provides useful comparisons with contrastive vision-language models. The supplementary material reports major training hyperparameters and prompt templates.
The paper is well organized, and the connection between holistic temporal structure, semantic caption generation, and discriminative grounding is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The claim of being “timestamp-free” is somewhat overstated. Training still uses ground-truth timestamps to construct segments, and inference ultimately converts frame assignments into temporal boundaries; the method avoids autoregressive timestamp generation rather than temporal boundary information altogether.

Query-focused captions are generated from ground-truth-cropped clips using MiniCPM-V and GPT-4o-mini. This introduces additional external semantic supervision that competing methods do not receive, so part of the gain may reflect enriched training targets rather than the proposed localization representation alone. A comparison giving equivalent caption supervision to stronger baseline variants would better isolate the contribution.

Important inference details are underspecified, particularly selection or tuning of the semantic-similarity threshold used for multi-segment retrieval. Results could be sensitive to this choice, yet no threshold sensitivity analysis or validation protocol is reported.

The partition formulation assigns every frame to exactly one structural-token instance and does not explain how overlapping, nested, or ambiguous event annotations are handled. This is a potentially important limitation for dense captioning and realistic temporal localization.
Results are reported without multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance analysis. Several smaller improvements, such as on Charades-STA, therefore have unclear robustness.

The comparison focuses primarily on video-LLM approaches and does not comprehensively position MeCo against strong specialist temporal-grounding and highlight-detection systems on the original benchmarks. Runtime, decoding cost, and memory are also unreported despite the additional caption-generation stage.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the displayed code-availability statement has no usable link, and some implementation choices—including exact output parsing, threshold calibration, and handling of malformed or incorrectly counted structural-token sequences—are not documented.

strengths: Presents a clear and meaningful alternative to timestamp-token generation: structural event/transition tokens, query-focused captions, and contrastive token-to-frame grounding form a coherent semantic localization framework.
Reports broad evaluation across multiple temporal grounding, highlight detection, dense captioning, and temporal reasoning tasks, with substantial improvements over prior video-LLM approaches.
Includes useful controlled comparisons using common base architectures and E.T.Instruct training, reducing—though not eliminating—confounding from model scale and training data.
Ablations separately examine transition tokens, query-focused captioning, query copying, grounding-loss variants, and compatibility with several boundary-centric strategies.
Strong results with multiple backbones, including competitive dataset-specific results against specialist models, suggest that the approach is not tied to one LLM.
The method, training pipeline, prompts, hyperparameters, inference pseudocode, and representative failure cases are documented reasonably well.
weaknesses: The principal comparisons remain partly confounded by additional supervision: MeCo receives ground-truth-window-conditioned captions produced by MiniCPM-V-2.6 and GPT-4o-mini, whereas competing E.T.Instruct models do not receive equivalent synthetic semantic annotations. The ablations show that QFC matters but do not fully separate architectural gains from teacher-generated supervision.

The framing that timestamp outputs fail to exploit semantic understanding is stronger than the evidence supports. Results demonstrate that this implementation works better under the tested settings, but do not establish the claimed general limitation of boundary-centric methods.

There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite several relatively small reported improvements. Hyperparameter and checkpoint-selection procedures are also insufficiently detailed to assess comparison variance.

Inference contains consequential heuristics that are only briefly described: discontinuous assignments are merged into multiple events, overlapping events require suppression of adjacent token scores, and dataset-specific fine-tuning changes the structural-token format to a single transition token. These deviations weaken the simplicity claim and are not ablated.

Comparing per-token probabilities normalized independently across time and then assigning each frame by an argmax can introduce calibration and segment-duration biases. The paper does not analyze this issue or compare against alternative decoding/segmentation procedures.

Fine-boundary accuracy remains weaker: on Charades-STA, the strongest MeCo variant trails TRACE at R@1 IoU 0.7 despite leading at looser thresholds. This limits the central temporal-localization contribution, where precise boundaries are important.

The paper does not report training/inference cost, autoregressive-caption latency, caption-generation cost, or sensitivity to caption quality, frame rate, token-count errors, and video duration. These omissions matter because MeCo adds generation before localization.

Some evaluation details are underspecified, including how thresholds for the contrastive baselines are selected and a sufficiently explicit accounting of possible source-dataset exposure behind every result labeled zero-shot.

strengths: The paper offers a clear alternative to direct timestamp generation: autoregressively generated event/transition tokens, query-focused captions, and contrastive frame-token grounding form a coherent framework.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering multiple localization, captioning, highlight-detection, and temporal-reasoning tasks, three model configurations, zero-shot transfer, and dataset-specific fine-tuning.

The controlled comparisons and component ablations generally support the usefulness of transition tokens, query-focused captioning, and frame-level grounding. The improvements are often large rather than merely incremental.
The method, inference procedure, training prompts, failure cases, and major hyperparameters are described reasonably well, and the paper candidly acknowledges weaker fine-boundary localization.
weaknesses: The central comparison between a semantic-oriented method and timestamp-oriented methods is significantly confounded. MeCo receives additional query-focused captions synthesized from ground-truth event clips using MiniCPM-V-2.6 and GPT-4o-mini, while many headline baselines do not receive equivalent enriched supervision. Thus, gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed representation.

Several supposedly controlled comparisons are not fully controlled. Adapting MeCo to the TimeChat/VTG-LLM setting changes the Q-Former and introduces bidirectional visual-token attention, while official-checkpoint comparisons mix architectures, dataset sizes, training epochs, model sizes, and training recipes.

The paper calls the framework “timestamp-free,” but training still requires ground-truth temporal boundaries to construct structural-token targets, generate captions from cropped event clips, and optimize frame-token grounding. The approach changes the output parameterization rather than removing timestamp supervision.

The grounding objective normalizes each structural token over time, whereas inference compares those independently normalized probabilities across structural tokens using an argmax. Such scores need not be calibrated across tokens because each has a different temporal partition function. This training-inference mismatch is neither justified nor ablated.

The structural-token generation component is insufficiently evaluated directly. There are no measurements of event-count accuracy, structural-token sequence accuracy, transition detection, sensitivity to token-generation errors, or oracle-token performance, despite token-count failures being an acknowledged failure mode.

Results are reported without repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance testing. This is particularly problematic for small differences and for comparisons based on the authors’ reimplementations.

The synthetic-caption pipeline lacks a systematic quality audit, filtering analysis, contamination discussion, and ablation separating richer supervision from caption-mediated reasoning. Dense-captioning gains are especially susceptible to this confound.

Important inference and evaluation choices remain underspecified, including handling of overlapping events, aggregation of multiple event-token scores for highlight detection, thresholding/post-processing choices, and behavior when no event token is generated. The prose and pseudocode also disagree in places about overlap handling and returned segment indices.

For dataset-specific fine-tuning, the method abandons the claimed temporally ordered structural representation and appends a single transition token attending to all background frames. This substantial task-dependent modification weakens the claimed unified formulation and is not adequately analyzed.

The code-availability footnote is blank in the submitted PDF, while reproducibility relies heavily on claimed supplementary code and generated data. The manuscript also contains numerous typographical and presentation errors.

strengths: Presents a clear and meaningful departure from timestamp-generation approaches: structural event/transition tokens, query-focused captions, and contrastive token-to-frame grounding form a coherent semantic-oriented framework.

The empirical results are strong and broad. MeCo improves substantially across nine E.T. Bench tasks and performs competitively on both Charades-STA and QVHighlights, including dataset-specific fine-tuning settings.

Evaluation includes several model backbones and controlled comparisons in which competing localization strategies use the same training data and base architecture, strengthening the attribution of gains to the proposed approach.
Ablations are informative and cover transition tokens, query-focused captions, query copying, grounding-loss variants, and the compatibility of captions with several boundary-centric methods.
The paper is well motivated, clearly organized, and unusually candid about weaker fine-boundary localization at high temporal-IoU thresholds.
Implementation details, training prompts, inference pseudocode, failure cases, and stated release of code/data provide a reasonably strong basis for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The inference rule is not fully justified: each structural token is independently normalized over time and the resulting probabilities are compared across tokens using argmax. These distributions need not be calibrated across tokens and can depend on segment duration; an ablation against unnormalized similarities or token-wise normalization is needed.

Query-focused captions are synthesized from ground-truth-trimmed event clips using MiniCPM-V and GPT-4o-mini. The paper does not quantify caption quality, hallucination rates, sensitivity to the caption generator, or the cost of constructing this additional supervision.

The method still relies heavily on timestamp annotations to construct event/transition labels and optimize frame-level grounding. Thus, claims of being “timestamp-free” or “completely” free of timestamps apply only to LLM output representation, not to training supervision.
Reported results lack confidence intervals or variation across training runs, making it difficult to assess the robustness of some smaller gains.
Boundary precision remains weaker at the strict Charades-STA R@1@0.7 metric, consistent with the method's coarse 1-fps sampling and semantic rather than boundary-focused design.

Efficiency is insufficiently characterized: there is no comparison of training cost, inference latency, memory use, or the overhead of autoregressively generating detailed captions before localization.
